At a stable thermal regime of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], the mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) was calculated as 2.8% [GSI = 2.8%]. This value suggests that this species does not invest an extreme proportion of its body reserves into a single spawning episode, instead adopting a strategy that likely spreads reproductive effort across several events within a breeding season. The measurement aligns with patterns observed in certain temperate sparids where gamete production represents a modest but consistent fraction of female body mass, allowing for iteroparous reproduction over an extended lifespan.

A comprehensive growth study relying on length-frequency analysis and otolith readings provided robust estimates of the species' maximum attainable dimensions and size at key life-history transitions. The ultimate standard length recorded for this species was 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], representing the theoretical maximum size approached by the oldest and slowest-growing individuals. In many fish species, the length at which 50 percent of the population reaches sexual maturity marks a critical ontogenetic benchmark, and for the Blue hottentot this value was determined to be a standard length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters]. This size threshold at puberty indicates that individuals require considerable somatic growth before directing resources toward gonadal development, a pattern typical of iteroparous teleosts inhabiting stable subtropical environments.

Body mass at birth, a parameter that is inherently difficult to measure directly for pelagic spawning species, was estimated from egg diameter data derived from a closely related congener, Acanthopagrus berda. Based on an assumed spherical egg with a diameter of 750 micrometers, the calculated wet weight at birth for a newly fertilized ovum of Pachymetopon aeneum is 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This minute initial mass underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high early-life mortality typical of the pelagic larval phase in marine fishes. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by adults, derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship, reaches 2516 grams [Wwi = 2516 grams] for individuals approaching the asymptotic length, a difference of several orders of magnitude that highlights the tremendous scope for growth during the juvenile and adult stages.

The wet weight at which puberty is attained provides a further perspective on the energetic prerequisites for reproduction in this sparid. Using the same length-weight conversion applied to the standard length at puberty, individuals are estimated to reach a body mass of 229 grams [Wwp = 229 grams] by the time they first become reproductively mature. This mass represents a critical nutritional threshold that must be surpassed before resources can be safely diverted toward gametogenesis. Field data indicate that females below this weight are rarely found to be gravid, suggesting a physiological constraint linking somatic energy reserves to the onset of vitellogenesis. The species thus appears to follow a size-based rather than strictly age-based maturation schedule, a life-history tactic that buffers against year-to-year variability in food availability by deferring reproduction until adequate body condition is achieved.

Maximum lifespan in the Blue hottentot has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and validated through otolith annulus counts conducted under consistent environmental conditions. At a water temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], which represents the approximate annual mean within its natural distribution along the South African coast, the maximum documented longevity reaches 4380 days [am = 4380 days]. This relatively long lifespan is typical of slow-growing, late-maturing sparids that invest in structural growth before committing to reproduction. The combination of delayed puberty, high ultimate body size, and extended reproductive tenure suggests that Pachymetopon aeneum operates under a conservative life-history strategy, where adult survival is prioritized over maximizing early reproductive output, a pattern well-suited to the temperate subtidal reefs it inhabits.
